title: Sen. Cortez Masto Pushes Landmark Bill to Shield DACA Recipients From Deportation
excerpt: The Fairness for Immigrant Families Act would require high-level approval before deporting parents of U.S. citizen children and expand relief from removal, as DACA renewal delays leave hundreds of thousands in limbo.
body:
• Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) is pushing the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act, which would expand cancellation of removal and require senior approval before deporting parents of U.S. citizen children
  • DHS reported that more than 260 DACA recipients were detained last year and at least 86 were deported, despite having active protections
  • The bill addresses notario fraud, establishes a National Office for New Americans, and creates reporting requirements on enforcement actions against DACA families
  • An estimated 530,000 DACA recipients currently face uncertainty as the Trump administration has been accused of deliberately slow-walking renewal applications

A Bill Born From Crisis

As the Trump administration intensifies immigration enforcement, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada is pressing her landmark legislation — the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act — designed to provide structural protections for DACA recipients and mixed-status families facing deportation.

The bill, which Cortez Masto first introduced in 2020 and has reintroduced in subsequent congressional sessions, takes aim at what advocates describe as systemic gaps in the immigration system that leave longtime residents vulnerable to removal despite having followed every rule.

"What the administration is doing to DACA recipients, to Dreamers, to their families, and even to the United States citizens goes against everything our nation was founded on."

— Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.)

What the Bill Would Do

The Fairness for Immigrant Families Act is a comprehensive package organized into three titles. Title I focuses on protecting immigrant families by removing barriers for long-term immigrants to become lawful permanent residents, eliminating bars to reentry, and reestablishing the 245(i) program for those with family ties to adjust their status.

The bill would make cancellation of removal more accessible by recognizing a wider range of family hardships and increasing the number of cancellations permitted each year. It would also establish an affirmative application process for cancellation of removal through USCIS, rather than requiring individuals to wait until they are already in removal proceedings.

A provision requiring high-level DHS approval before any parent of a U.S. citizen child is deported directly addresses cases like that of Maria de Jesús Estrada Juárez, a DACA recipient who was unlawfully deported earlier this year and only returned following a federal judge's ruling.

Title II tackles notario fraud — schemes where individuals misrepresent themselves as immigration attorneys — by criminalizing fraudulent immigration services and creating FTC enforcement mechanisms. Title III establishes reporting requirements on enforcement actions and protections for immigrants who are crime victims or witnesses.

DACA Recipients Under Siege

The bill's urgency has sharpened as DACA recipients face what advocates describe as a two-pronged assault: aggressive enforcement and bureaucratic delays that effectively strip protections.

According to data obtained by NBC News from a DHS letter sent to Cortez Masto, more than 260 DACA recipients were detained between January and December of last year, and at least 86 were deported. Many had submitted renewal applications on time but saw their status expire while in detention.

Juan Sebastian Chavez Velasco submitted his DACA renewal in November but was arrested in February while driving to visit his newborn U.S. citizen daughter in the NICU. His DACA expired on March 10 while he remained in detention, separated from his family.

"My husband did everything he was asked to do. He applied on time, followed the rules, and built a life here with our family. But because of these delays, his status expired while he was in detention."

— Stephanie Villareal, wife of detained DACA recipient

Slow-Walking as Strategy

Cortez Masto and fellow Democratic senators have accused DHS of deliberately slow-walking DACA renewal processing. Earlier this year, she led 40 Democratic senators in demanding the department address backlogs that push otherwise eligible individuals out of the workforce simply because their applications are not adjudicated in time.

"DHS, because of their punitive deportation plan, are slow-walking this intentionally so they can use this as a change of circumstance for these DACA recipients," Cortez Masto told NOTUS. "It really is a betrayal of the system, a betrayal of a community who has faithfully trusted the United States government."

Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, said the delays create instability that neither families nor employers can absorb. "These are individuals who followed the rules, submitted their applications on time, and are now being separated from their families because of attacks on immigrants with work authorizations and processing delays entirely outside of their control."

What Lies Ahead

The bill faces steep odds in the current political environment, where immigration enforcement has broad support in Congress. But Cortez Masto — the first and only Latina senator — has positioned the legislation as a test of whether the system will honor its commitments to those who complied with its rules.

For the estimated 530,000 active DACA recipients, the stakes are immediate. Without legislative action, they remain dependent on a renewal process that advocates say the administration has weaponized. The Fairness for Immigrant Families Act would not grant DACA recipients permanent status, but it would close loopholes that allow the government to effectively revoke protections through administrative delay.
nri_angle: DACA protections are critical for hundreds of thousands of immigrants who were brought to the U.S. as children, including many from South Asian families who have built lives and careers in America.
